I wrote this trying to sound compelling. That’s why I refer these disappointments as “reasons” of dropping out. I apologize for the confusion! But the only reason why I am dropping out is to pursue Compassers!

I am quitting college and I wanted to share the story of why I came to this conclusion (the main reason of dropping out is to pursue my true dreams = Compassers). My school, Virginia Tech, is known for its beautiful campus, massive football stadium, mouth-watering campus food, top-notch engineering programs, and being sustainable.

All these factors lured me into enrolling in Virginia Tech. But after two years, I realized… It wasn’t worth it.

The first major disappointment came during freshman orientation. While the orientation allowed me to explore the school before entering, it was clear to me that Virginia Tech was trying to leech off additional money from her consumers. Let me explain:

Upon acceptance to the school, I was required to pay a fee of $175 for the orientation. It was, of course, nonrefundable. The school simply increased the incentives of students to partake in the orientation. The logic is this: you already paid, so it would be a waste if you didn’t attend the orientation.

By half-forcing the students to participate, Virginia Tech successfully gained at least one or two additional customers: family members. Students aren’t going to come to the orientation alone! The family is going to obviously tag along. That means the family needs to at least spend money on hotel, gas, and food. And guess what? The school advertises the crap out of their school gears during the orientation. And it works. New students and their family members are all wearing their new and shiny school gears. They also make you buy the software that you may already own. I’m not joking. They literally package all of those software together into your tuition. No loopholes. You got to pay for them.

My second major disappointment was caused by Virginia Tech’s lack of willingness to efficiently communicate with her customers (AKA students). Here’s how the story goes. I purchased a commuter’s parking pass in order to commute from my apartment and park on campus. While finding a parking lot was very difficult, the parking pass was still extremely valuable as it allowed me to commute without too much hassle. Unfortunately, the value of the parking pass depreciated extremely quickly.

Virginia Tech announced that they would be building a new campus building in one of the busiest student commuter’s parking lot. This announcement occurred very abruptly; it was during the middle of the fall semester. Virginia Tech barely made any visible announcements to the commuters. They should have told the students the possibility of a construction in the middle of the parking lot before the students purchased the parking pass. If the customers knew about the fact that the quantity and the quality of the service they were purchasing was going to depreciate in the middle of their subscription, they would have valued the parking pass much differently. I was extremely disappointed when Virginia Tech gave an abrupt two-week notice before closing down the parking lot. I mean, closing the parking lot shouldn’t be as simple as quitting your part-time job. Two-week notices are for quitting your job at McDonald’s. They are definitely not suitable for changing the lifestyle of thousands of customers. And indeed, commuting to school became more difficult and chaotic.

My third major disappointment rose to surface as I realized it was almost impossible to make a positive change within the school system. Here is how this story goes.

Virginia Tech has a facility called the Math Emporium outside the main part of the campus. It is equipped with 537 iMac computers and inefficient light bulbs (250W) that buzz all day long. In other words, it consumes a lot of energy. Unfortunately, the facility keeps everything running even when the facility is not available to staffs and students. The facility wastes a lot of energy unnecessarily. I wanted to fix this issue, but it was impossible. The bureaucratic process that I was required to go through was simply too much compared to the simplicity of what I was asking them to do. I just wanted them to save some energy by changing the light policy.

After acquiring these information, I wanted to know how “Environmental-friendly” Virginia Tech was. Surprisingly, Virginia Tech was given a gold rating by “STARS” program of AASHE. I was shocked and confused. How could this school waste so much energy, yet receive a gold rating from an institution that cares about environment?

It turns out Virginia Tech was able to conveniently include and exclude Math Emporium as part of their campus at their convenience. For example, during freshman orientation and public announcements, Math Emporium is regarded as part of the campus. I remember my orientation leader telling me that Emporium is considered part of the campus since it’s well connected to the main part of the campus. He also asserted that commuting from and to the Math Emporium is extremely convenient, so it was “practically” part of Virginia Tech’s campus. Nonetheless, when it comes to energy assessing, Virginia Tech does not include the energy usage of the Math Emporium as part of their energy consumption. Hence, it becomes relatively easier for Virginia Tech to receive “Gold” ratings. Sadly, Virginia Tech boasts about their “Gold” rating status and describes themselves as “Environmental-Friendly” school all the time. False-advertisement at its finest.

As you can see, these are the three major disappointments that I experienced while attending Virginia Tech. It certainly is not why I am quitting college (I do have an agenda and a dream that I will be pursuing), but these three reasons played some roles. I strongly felt that while students thought of college as a school, college institutions were treating students like their customers. It seems like colleges are taking advantage of high school graduates who lack the realization to see college as a business. And by the time one realizes this fact, individuals are already in massive debt.

Think of it this way. If you were paying to stay at an all-inclusive hotel, you would expect to receive every meal for free. That would be your right as a customer at an all-inclusive hotel. If you were rejected of a meal that you already purchased, you would complain and call the management to fix that issue. Why aren’t students doing this against schools? Why do we treat colleges as schools when colleges see us as a method of expanding their profits? If they are going to treat us as customers, we should treat colleges more like an all-inclusive hotel.

Third-party businesses are also an enormous issue. Think of publication firms. They have successfully inflated the price of textbooks at an insane rate over the past decade. Put it this way. Let’s say the cost of a college ruled notebook was $5 ten years ago. Let’s also say that the cost of a biology textbook was $30 ten years ago. Now let’s move ten years forward. The cost of a college ruled notebook inflated and became $7 while the cost of a biology textbook became $230. We don’t even have to do the math. Inflation rate of college textbooks is definitely higher than the inflation rate of a college ruled notebook. Why do we accept this fact casually when the material that makes both of the products are almost equal? In fact, the inflation rate of college textbook is insanely higher than the inflation rate of the majority of the products that we consume daily.

We need to stop businesses from abusing us under the name of “education.” We, as a society, became too afraid to learn outside of an institution. All the great men from the past learned outside of institutions. They learned and were inspired by what this planet provided them with. Textbooks and institutions should just be a resource. Not something that is required in our lifetime.

I am leaving. But my education won’t stop.

source: http://compassers.com/2015/07/22/i-quit-virginia-tech-here-are-the-reasons/

I'm hoping this means there's now more to the theory, but for me it takes away the anxiety of finding out matter can literally be destroyed from matter and antimatter touching. Too many sleepless nights.

Yes. This is a well-known prediction of QED.

They have a design for a photon collider that should produce e+e- pairs. That's never been done before.

While it is certainly true that this interaction is taking place during the big bang (e+ + e- < -> 2 photons freezes out of equilibrium when the Universe has a temperature of about 0.5 MeV, and is the last standard model interaction to freeze out of the plasma), this interaction was discovered long before then. The reverse direction of the interaction discussed in this article, e+ + e- -> 2 photons, has been known to conserve Energy since the early 1930's. That conservation of energy is a clear indication that the interaction obeys time reversal symmetry (c.f. Noether's theorem). This means that the reverse interaction, 2 photons -> e+ + e- , will proceed with exactly the same amplitude.

The fact that no one has built a machine that would generate particle-antiparticle pairs from light before is not related to our uncertainty that the interaction is real. It's simply a technical matter that herding photons of sufficient energy and density to perform the experiment is very difficult compared to collecting leptons or baryons into lumps and smashing them into eachother.

Brush with her. When you are brushing try to make it seem like fun.

Honestly, I just keep very calm, hold her firmly, and made it a routine. I found persistence works, just keep putting the brush in and brushing until she kind of gives up. Yup had the same problem here. Our tactic was to fully involve her in the process.

She got to pick one of two toothbrushes put on the paste and brush herself (read. suck on the toothbrush) for the first ten seconds. Then one of us takes over. Pretty smooth sailing from there on out with the occasional crying of course but no more bat out of hell.

We have a flashing tooth brush, which when it goes off signals when to stop brushing.

We play a game like this.

Me: Wait a second, I think I see some squirrel toes in there. Are there squirrel toes in there?

Child: Laugh, squeal, etc.

Me: Holy cow! I see monkey ears. Do you have monkey ears stuck between your teeth?

Child: No! Laugh, squeal, etc.

Anyway it just keeps going with me coming up with all sort of weird/gross stuff I see in her mouth. Pretty soon she's laughing it up and between her laughing and her allowing me to brush the spider legs out of her teeth, it goes Ok.
Thanks. Never hurts to try more silliness!
